text: On 1 May, people give each other sprigs of a small white flower, sold on every street corner.
note: 'Le muguet' (lily of the valley) brings luck; on 1 May anyone may sell it in the street without a licence.

text: One evening in late May, a whole apartment block has drinks and snacks together in the courtyard.
note: 'La Fête des voisins' (neighbours' day) started in 1999 and now draws millions; everyone brings something to share.

text: It's normal to wish people "happy new year" right up to the end of January.
note: 'Bonne année!' and New Year cards ('cartes de vœux') aren't considered late until 31 January.

text: Around New Year, people give an envelope of cash to the building caretaker and the postman.
note: 'Les étrennes': a few euros for the postie, more for a helpful concierge. The habit is slowly fading.

text: In late autumn, firefighters knock on your door to sell you next year's calendar.
note: The money goes to their charity fund; postal workers sell calendars too. Some cities have restricted it because of fakes.

text: Young kids often have no school on Wednesdays, so that's the day for clubs and sport.
note: A free Wednesday dates back to the 1880s school laws; many primary schools still run a four-day week.

text: Grumbling about anything is jokingly called the national sport.
note: 'Râler' (to grumble) bonds strangers: moaning about the trains together counts as small talk.

text: Replying "not great" to good news can actually mean it's brilliant.
note: 'Pas terrible' used ironically is a classic of 'second-degree' (ironic) humour.

text: Unsure if someone is joking, you ask "is that second-degree?"
note: 'C'est du second degré?': first degree is literal, second degree is ironic. Friends tease each other in the second degree.

text: A corny groaner of a joke is named after the jokes printed inside sweet wrappers.
note: 'Une blague Carambar': the caramel bars carry puns like 'I thought Mozart was dead, but mozzarella'.

text: About one hair salon in ten has a pun for a name.
note: Built on 'tif' (slang for hair) and the English 'hair': 'Créa'tif' alone is used by over a hundred salons.

text: A heated argument over dinner means it was a good evening, not a ruined one.
note: Having an opinion and defending it is expected; lively disagreement is part of the entertainment.

text: Arriving at the office, you greet each colleague one by one before sitting down.
note: At least a 'bonjour' or 'salut' to each person; heading straight to your desk can seem rude.

text: Saying "good morning" twice to the same colleague in one day is a small faux pas.
note: The second time, it's a nod or a joking 'rebonjour' (hello again).

text: When someone leaves the company, they throw a small drinks-and-snacks party at the office.
note: 'Le pot de départ'. There are welcome pots and end-of-year pots too; the Dutch call it an 'afscheidsborrel'.

text: Throughout January, colleagues share a crown cake at the office.
note: Many companies pay for 'la galette' at work, and whoever finds the trinket gets the paper crown.

text: Even short work emails end with "cordially" before your name.
note: 'Cordialement' is the default; 'bien à vous' is warmer. Signing off with just your name looks abrupt.

text: In meetings everyone is expected to speak up, so they tend to run long.
note: Staying silent (unless you're new) can make you look uninvolved; debate is how decisions are made.

text: Slipping out of a party without saying goodbye is called "leaving the English way".
note: 'Filer à l'anglaise'. Poles and Ukrainians say the same, while the English call it 'French leave'.

text: To faint is "to fall into the apples".
note: 'Tomber dans les pommes', probably a mangled form of the old verb 'se pâmer' (to swoon).

text: Feeling down is "having the cockroach".
note: 'Avoir le cafard': the poet Baudelaire helped make it popular.

text: Something that will never happen will happen "when hens have teeth".
note: 'Quand les poules auront des dents', the local 'when pigs fly'.

text: To speed up in a car, you "press on the mushroom".
note: 'Appuyer sur le champignon': the accelerator pedal of early cars looked like a mushroom.

text: When you give up on a riddle, you "give your tongue to the cat".
note: 'Je donne ma langue au chat' means 'I give up, tell me'.

text: Heavy rain is "raining ropes".
note: 'Il pleut des cordes': the rain falls in lines so straight they look like ropes.

text: Calling someone you love "my cabbage" or "my flea" is sweet, not an insult.
note: 'Mon chou', 'ma puce', 'mon lapin' (my rabbit): food and animals rule the pet names.

text: Young people flip the syllables of words around as slang.
note: 'Verlan' comes from 'l'envers' (backwards): fête becomes 'teuf', fou becomes 'ouf', merci becomes 'cimer'.

text: Almost every sentence gets a filler that literally means "suddenly".
note: 'Du coup' now just means 'so', and parents beg teenagers to use it less.

text: Shop staff and doctors narrate what they do with little sounds like "hop!" and "toc!".
note: Said while handing something over or finishing a move; columnists joke the country is split between 'hop' and 'toc' people.

text: Instead of "good luck", people wish you "good courage" before a chore or an exam.
note: 'Bon courage!' means 'hang in there': it's about effort, not luck, and it's said for anything from exams to tax forms.

text: "There you go" ends stories, sentences and shop visits, usually with a shrug.
note: 'Voilà' (and 'voilà quoi') wraps up almost anything, no magician's flourish needed.

text: In many buildings, the lift shows "F" instead of a 4 for the fourth floor.
note: 'Sa' sounds like both 'four' and 'death', so the number is avoided; flats with several 4s in the number can be harder to sell.

text: In restaurants you press a buzzer on the table or simply call out "over here!" to get a waiter.
note: 'Yeogiyo!' (here!) is normal, not rude; nobody waits to catch a server's eye.

text: You can have fried chicken delivered to your spot on the grass in a riverside park.
note: Han River picnickers order to special 'delivery zones'; food delivery is so old that a 1768 diary mentions lunch sent to an office.

text: Public bins are rare, so people carry their rubbish home.
note: Street bins mostly disappeared when strict pay-per-bag recycling came in; a few remain in tourist areas.

text: Homes keep a separate pair of plastic slippers just for the bathroom.
note: Bathrooms are wet rooms, so 'yokshil sillipeo' (bathroom slippers) wait by the door, even for a 3 am visit.

text: Electric fans come with sleep timers, because a fan running all night in a closed room is said to be dangerous.
note: The 'fan death' belief goes back to a 1927 newspaper scare; younger people mostly joke about it now.

text: Waiters cut noodles and grilled meat with kitchen scissors right at your table.
note: Scissors ('gawi') are a normal table tool; servers snip long noodles into portions for you.

text: Instead of tips, a restaurant you visit often brings you a free extra and calls it "service".
note: 'Seobiseu' means a freebie, like a drink or an extra dish. Tipping simply isn't done.

text: Jiggling your leg under the table is said to shake your luck and money away.
note: Elders will tell you to stop: 'dari tteolji ma, bok naganda' (don't shake your leg, your luck will leave).

text: Whistling at night is avoided, because it's said to call ghosts and snakes.
note: Whistle in daylight only: at night it supposedly summons 'gwisin' (ghosts).

text: Writing someone's name in red ink is a big no-no.
note: Names of the dead were traditionally written in red, so a living person's name in red is a bad omen.

text: Before a big exam, students are given sticky toffee so the answers "stick".
note: 'Yeot' (rice taffy) helps you 'stick' to a pass; parents even press it onto school gates before the national exam.

text: Couples celebrate their 100th day together, and often the 200th and 300th too.
note: Couples count days, not months; 'baegil' (100 days) brings gifts, letters and often matching rings.

text: On 11 November, couples and friends swap chocolate-dipped biscuit sticks.
note: 11/11 looks like four sticks; 'Pepero Day' topped a 2024 survey of favourite 'days'.

text: Singles have their own day in April, when they eat black-bean noodles together.
note: On 'Black Day' (14 April), those who got nothing on 14 February or 14 March eat 'jjajangmyeon', half in solidarity, half as a joke.

text: At their first birthday, babies pick an object from a tray that "predicts" their future job.
note: 'Doljabi': a stethoscope means doctor, thread a long life, money wealth. Ukraine has a similar first-birthday grab.

text: At New Year, children kneel and bow deeply to their elders, then get cash in envelopes.
note: 'Sebae' (the bow) is answered with 'sebaetdon' (bow money) and a wish for a lucky year.

text: Young people joke about putting a price on each nosy question relatives ask at holidays.
note: The 'nagging menu': 'Found a job yet?' costs one price, 'When are you getting married?' more, and 'Kids?' the most.

text: On Parents' Day, children pin red carnations on mum and dad.
note: There's one shared Parents' Day (8 May) instead of separate Mother's and Father's Days.

text: Wedding guests hand a cash envelope to a desk at the door and get a meal ticket back.
note: The reception desk records each gift, and the ticket gets you into the buffet, often on another floor.

text: The ceremony takes about 30 minutes, and guests can drop off their gift, eat and leave.
note: Wedding halls run back-to-back slots, so skipping the vows and heading for the buffet is perfectly normal.

text: The classic housewarming gift is a giant pack of toilet paper.
note: It's wordplay: 'pullida' means both 'to unroll' and 'to go smoothly'. Laundry detergent ('may your luck foam up') is the runner-up.

text: Whoever is oldest or most senior at the table is expected to pay for everyone.
note: Traditionally 'the senior pays'; it's changing fast, as most people under 30 now split the bill with friends.

text: Nobody picks up their spoon until the eldest person at the table starts eating.
note: The same goes for a work lunch with the boss: wait for the senior's first bite.

text: Anything you hand to an older person, from a plate to a card, is passed with both hands.
note: Two hands, or the left hand supporting the right forearm, shows respect; one hand looks careless.

text: You never stand your chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice.
note: It looks like the offering table set for the dead, so it reads as a funeral gesture.

text: You don't pour your own drink: you fill your neighbour's glass and they fill yours.
note: Pour for elders with two hands; the rule applies to juice and water too.

text: Lots of small side dishes arrive free with every meal, and refills are free too.
note: 'Banchan' come unasked and are shared by the whole table.

text: "Have you eaten?" is a casual hello, and the right answer is just "yes".
note: 'Bap meogeosseoyo?' works like 'how are you?'; 'bap' (rice) stands for any meal.

text: Before eating you say "I will eat well", and afterwards "I ate well", to whoever cooked or paid.
note: 'Jal meokgetseumnida' / 'jal meogeotseumnida' are a thank-you, not a wish to the others like 'enjoy your meal'.

text: People say "our mum", "our house" and "our company", even when it's just theirs.
note: 'Uri' (our) replaces 'my' for things you belong to: 'uri eomma', 'uri jip'. People who live alone say it too.

text: Women call an older male friend "big brother", even when they aren't related.
note: 'Oppa' is for an older brother or a close older guy, and also what many women call their boyfriend.

text: Strictly speaking, your "friend" is someone born in the same year as you.
note: 'Chingu' means a same-age peer; someone a year older becomes 'hyeong', 'nuna', 'oppa' or 'eonni'.

text: Taxi drivers and customers get an honorific added to their role, like "honoured driver".
note: '-nim' is added to roles: 'gisanim' (driver), 'gogaengnim' (customer), 'seonsaengnim' (teacher).

text: People cheer each other on by shouting the English word "fighting!"
note: 'Hwaiting!' means 'you can do it!' and is shouted before exams, games and presentations.

text: There's a single word for eating out alone, and it's a whole lifestyle.
note: 'Honbap' = 'hon' (alone) + 'bap' (meal); restaurants now have counters and menus for solo diners.

text: Groan-worthy puns are so popular they have a name: "middle-aged-uncle gags".
note: 'Ajae gag': 'What's a king's bean?' King + 'kong' (bean) = King Kong. Americans call them 'dad jokes'.

text: "Are you a T?" is a teasing put-down for someone who's being cold or too logical.
note: From personality tests: T (thinking) vs F (feeling). A comedy channel made it viral in 2023.

text: Asking for someone's four-letter personality type is normal first-meeting small talk.
note: 'MBTI mwoyeyo?' is everywhere, from dating profiles to job chats; it replaced the older blood-type small talk.

text: "Latte is horse" is a jokey way to tease a boss who starts a "back in my day" story.
note: It puns on 'na ttaeneun mariya' (in my day...): 'latte' sounds like 'na ttae', and 'mal' means both horse and speech.

text: Everyone has heard of "mum's friend's son", the perfect kid you're always compared to.
note: 'Eomchina' has top grades, a great job and perfect manners. Ukrainians joke about the same mum's-friend's-son.

text: One of the first things a new acquaintance asks is what year you were born.
note: The birth year sets who speaks politely to whom and who becomes 'big brother' or 'big sister'.

text: Many people still give two ages: their "real" one and a year or two more.
note: Under the old system you were 1 at birth and everyone aged on 1 January. It was officially dropped in 2023, but many still use it socially.

text: At work, you call your manager by job title plus an honorific, never by first name.
note: 'Gwajang-nim' (section chief) or 'Kim daeri-nim'. Some start-ups use English nicknames to flatten this.

text: Leaving the office before your boss calls for a quick bow and an apologetic "I'll go in first".
note: 'Meonjeo deureogagetseumnida'. A shorter legal work week eased the pressure, but the phrase remains.

text: Colleagues end the day by telling each other "you worked hard", even after a slow day.
note: 'Sugohasyeotseumnida' is the standard office goodbye, more thanks than praise.

text: Who's senior depends on who joined first, even if the other person is older.
note: 'Seonbae' (senior) and 'hubae' (junior) are set by school year or company entry; seniors look after juniors.

text: When shaking hands with a senior, you support your right forearm with your left hand.
note: A two-handed show of respect, often with a slight bow.

text: For the big holidays, companies give staff gift boxes of canned ham, cooking oil or toothpaste.
note: 'Seonmul set' (gift sets) for the autumn harvest holiday and New Year; a box of canned ham is a prized, joked-about classic.

text: "That might be a bit difficult" is how a polite "no" sounds at work.
note: Direct refusals are avoided to protect 'kibun' (mood, face); a long pause also means no.
